tips.title: Surface area grows slower than volume
tips.body: Double a cube's side and its **surface area ×4** but its **volume ×8**. So the **ratio halves**. That single fact is why big organisms need lungs and a bloodstream and an amoeba does not — and it is the answer to almost every *why do multicellular organisms need...* question.

tips.title: Four alveolus adaptations, four reasons
tips.body: **Large surface area**, **thin walls** (short diffusion distance), **good blood supply** and **ventilation** — the last two both **maintain the concentration gradient**. Give the reason with each; the adaptation on its own is only a description.

tips.title: Fick is a proportionality: factors or arbitrary units
tips.body: Rate $\propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness}}$. For a change, multiply for the top and divide for the bottom: the answer is a factor, *the rate doubles*, *the rate halves*. Substituting values gives a rate in **arbitrary units**, never in m/s or any other real unit, because the constant is left out.

tips.title: Thickness is on the bottom
tips.body: Surface area and concentration difference are on the **top**: more of either means a **faster** rate. **Thickness of membrane** is on the **bottom**: more of it means a **slower** rate. Treating thickness like the other two reverses the answer.

tips.title: Six substances to transport
tips.body: The spec names them: **oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, dissolved food molecules, mineral ions and urea**. A question asking what has to be transported wants examples from that list rather than *food and air*.

why.matters:
Every cell needs oxygen delivered and carbon dioxide taken away, and for a single cell diffusion does the whole job. For anything bigger it cannot, and the reason is geometry rather than biology.

Surface area grows as a **square** and volume as a **cube**, so as a thing gets bigger its surface falls behind what its insides need. Every exchange surface in this unit — alveoli, villi, root hairs, gills — is the same answer to that one problem: fold the surface up until it is big enough again.

examples.title: Why nothing large is a single cell
examples.body:
Take a cube of side 1 and its surface area to volume ratio is **6 : 1**. Double the side and the area goes up four times while the volume goes up eight, so the ratio **halves**. Double it again and it halves again.

That is why an amoeba can live on diffusion and you cannot. A large organism has far too little surface for its bulk, and the middle of it would be too far from the outside in any case — so it has to grow a specialised exchange surface and a transport system to reach it.

props.caption: Surface area to volume, for cubes of side 1, 2 and 4

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing how the surface area to volume ratio falls as a cube grows: six to one at side one, three to one at side two and one point five to one at side four

examples.title: A room-sized surface, folded into your chest
examples.body:
Your skin is about **1.8 m²**. The lining of your lungs, counted alveolus by alveolus, is about **70 m²** — around **39 times** as much, inside a space you can put your arms round.

Folding is how that is done, and the other three adaptations make each fold count: walls **one cell thick**, so the diffusion distance is tiny; a dense **capillary network** that carries oxygen away as fast as it arrives; and **ventilation**, which replaces the air. The last two do the same job — they keep the concentration difference steep.

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion comparing about seventy square metres of alveolar surface inside the lungs with about one point eight square metres of skin outside the body

examples.title: Why a fish suffocates in air
examples.body:
A fish out of water is surrounded by far more oxygen than it has ever had, and it suffocates. The gills are the reason: in water they are held apart by it, and in air the filaments **stick together and collapse**.

Fick's law says the rate depends on surface area and concentration difference divided by thickness. The concentration difference has gone up and the surface area has all but vanished, and the surface area is winning. It is the clearest case of a relationship being worth more than its parts: you can predict this without knowing anything about fish.

visual.alt: A table of Fick's law: surface area and concentration difference are on the top of the relationship and membrane thickness on the bottom, and for a fish in air the surface area collapses while the concentration difference rises

steps.title: What has to be moved, and why it is a problem
steps.body:
**Every organism has to move substances in and out.** The spec names six:

- **oxygen** — in, for respiration
- **carbon dioxide** — out, as a waste product of respiration
- **water** — both ways
- **dissolved food molecules** — in, from digestion
- **mineral ions** — in
- **urea** — out, as a waste product of breaking down excess amino acids

**For a single-celled organism this is easy.** Every part of it is close to the outside, so **diffusion alone** is fast enough. An amoeba needs no lungs, no blood and no heart.

**For anything larger, diffusion alone fails**, and for two reasons that work together:

1. The **distance** from the outside to the middle is far greater, and diffusion over a long distance is **very slow**.
2. The **surface area to volume ratio** is much **smaller**, so there is far less surface available for each unit of the body that needs supplying.

**So multicellular organisms need two things**: **exchange surfaces**, which are specialised for getting substances across, and a **transport system** to carry them the rest of the way. Lungs are the exchange surface; the **circulatory system** is the transport system.

**Plants face the same problem.** A plant takes in **water and mineral ions** through the **root hair cells** in its roots, and exchanges **carbon dioxide and oxygen** with the air through its **leaves**. Its transport tissues, **xylem** and **phloem**, carry substances between the two.

That is the logic of the whole unit, and it starts with a ratio.

steps.title: Surface area to volume ratio
steps.body:
**Spec point 8.2 asks for the calculation**, and it is the calculation that explains the biology.

For a **cube of side $s$**: the surface area is $6s^2$ — six square faces — and the volume is $s^3$. The ratio is one divided by the other.

**Watch what happens as the cube grows.** The surface area is a **square** and the volume is a **cube**, so the volume grows **faster**. Doubling the side multiplies the area by **4** and the volume by **8**, so the **ratio halves**.

steps.title: The alveoli
steps.body:
**The alveoli are the exchange surface of the lungs**, and spec point 8.3 asks how they are adapted for **gas exchange by diffusion between the air in the lungs and the blood in the capillaries**.

**Four adaptations, each with its reason:**

- **A very large surface area.** There are millions of alveoli, so there is far more surface for diffusion than a single sac would give.
- **Walls one cell thick**, and the capillary wall is one cell thick too — so the **diffusion distance is very short**.
- **A rich blood supply.** A dense network of capillaries carries oxygen away as fast as it arrives, which **keeps the concentration gradient steep**.
- **Ventilation.** Breathing replaces the air in the alveoli, bringing in fresh oxygen and removing carbon dioxide, which also **maintains the gradient**.

**Notice the last two have the same reason**, and that is the point: a gradient is only useful while it lasts. If the blood stopped flowing, oxygen would build up in it until diffusion stopped; if breathing stopped, the oxygen in the alveoli would run down until diffusion stopped. **Both** keep the difference large.

**The alveoli are also moist**, because gases must **dissolve** before they can diffuse across the membrane.

**Which way each gas goes.** Air in the alveoli is **higher** in oxygen than the blood arriving, so **oxygen diffuses into the blood**. That blood is **higher** in carbon dioxide than the air, so **carbon dioxide diffuses out** into the alveoli. Both are moving **down their own gradients** — and they move in **opposite directions** at the same time, which is worth stating deliberately.

steps.title: What affects the rate of diffusion
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* Three factors affect the rate of diffusion (spec point 8.4B):

- **Surface area** — a larger area means **more** diffusion at once, so a **faster** rate.
- **Concentration gradient** — a **bigger difference** between the two sides means a **faster** rate.
- **Diffusion distance** — a **thicker** membrane means a **slower** rate, because there is further to travel.

**Two of these speed things up and one slows them down**, and keeping that straight is the whole skill. Surface area and concentration difference are things you want **more** of. Distance is something you want **less** of.

**Every alveolus adaptation is one of these three**, which is why the two spec points sit together:

- millions of alveoli → **surface area**
- walls one cell thick → **diffusion distance**
- blood supply and ventilation → **concentration gradient**

So the adaptations are not a list to memorise. They are **three factors**, each addressed in the most effective way the body can manage.

**And the same three explain disease.** In emphysema the walls between alveoli break down, so there are **fewer, larger** air sacs and the **surface area falls**. In pneumonia fluid collects in the alveoli, so the **diffusion distance rises**. Both slow gas exchange, and naming which factor changed is what a question is after.

steps.title: Fick's law
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* Spec point 8.5B puts the three factors into one relationship:

$$\text{rate of diffusion} \propto \frac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness of membrane}}$$

**Read the position of each quantity.** Surface area and concentration difference are on the **top**, so increasing either **increases** the rate. Thickness is on the **bottom**, so increasing it **decreases** the rate.

**It is a proportionality.** There is no constant to look up, and it can be used in two ways.

- **By what factor does the rate change?** Multiply for changes on the top and divide for changes on the bottom. The answer is a factor, such as *6 times as fast*, with no unit.
- **Calculate the rate from values.** Substitute them: surface area × concentration difference ÷ thickness. The answer is a rate in **arbitrary units**. It lets you compare one surface with another, but it is not in m/s or any real unit, because the constant has been left out.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The ratio argument is the spine of this whole unit.** Surface area grows as a **square** and volume as a **cube**, so volume always wins. Doubling a cube's side multiplies area by **4** and volume by **8**: the ratio **halves**. A large organism therefore has proportionally **less** surface through which to supply proportionally **more** body — and diffusion, which is also slow over long distances, cannot keep up. Both halves of that argument, the **ratio** and the **distance**, are worth giving.

**Give the reason with every adaptation.** *Large surface area* is a description; *large surface area, so more diffusion can happen at once* is an explanation. An *explain* question wants the second half of each pair.

**Blood supply and ventilation are the same answer twice.** Both **maintain the concentration gradient**, one from the blood side and one from the air side. Seeing them as one idea rather than two facts is what lets you explain an unfamiliar case — why a fish ventilates its gills, why a resting person exchanges gas more slowly than a running one.

**In Fick's law, position tells you direction.** Top: **surface area** and **concentration difference** — more is **faster**. Bottom: **thickness** — more is **slower**. The reliable check is to make the two cancel: doubling the area **and** the thickness leaves the rate **unchanged**, so if your method does not give 1 for that case, it is the wrong way up.

**Know what kind of answer it gives.** Fick's law is a **proportionality**: there is no constant. A question about a change wants a **factor**, and *the rate becomes six times as fast* is a complete answer. Substituted values give a rate in **arbitrary units**; attaching m/s or any real unit has misread the symbol.

**Disease questions are factor questions.** Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so **surface area falls**. Pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid, so **diffusion distance rises**. Asthma narrows airways, so **ventilation falls** and with it the **gradient**. Naming which of the three factors has changed turns an unfamiliar condition into a question you have already practised.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Organisms must transport **oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, dissolved food molecules, mineral ions and urea**.
- A **single-celled** organism manages by **diffusion alone**: short distances and a large surface area to volume ratio.
- **Surface area grows as a square, volume as a cube**, so the **ratio falls** as an organism gets bigger.
- For a cube of side $s$: surface area $= 6s^2$, volume $= s^3$.
- Side 1 → **6 : 1**. Side 2 → **3 : 1**. Side 3 → **2 : 1**. Side 4 → **1.5 : 1**.
- So multicellular organisms need **exchange surfaces** and a **transport system**.
- **Alveoli**: millions of them give a **large surface area**.
- **Walls one cell thick**, and capillary walls one cell thick, give a **short diffusion distance**.
- A **rich blood supply** and **ventilation** both **maintain the concentration gradient**.
- The lining is **moist**, because gases must **dissolve** to diffuse.
- **Oxygen** diffuses **into** the blood and **carbon dioxide out**, each down its **own** gradient, at the same time.
- *(Biology only.)* Rate of diffusion (8.4B) depends on **surface area**, **concentration gradient** and **diffusion distance**.
- *(Biology only.)* Fick's law (8.5B): rate $\propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness}}$.
- **Top means faster, bottom means slower.** Answers are **factors**, or rates in **arbitrary units** when values are substituted.
- **Emphysema** reduces **surface area**; **pneumonia** increases **diffusion distance**.

questions.prompt: Explain why a single-celled organism needs no transport system, but a large multicellular animal needs both exchange surfaces and a circulatory system. Use surface area to volume ratio in your answer.
questions.solution:
A single-celled organism such as an amoeba needs no transport system because **diffusion alone is fast enough**. No part of it is far from the surface, so the **diffusion distance** is tiny, and its **surface area to volume ratio** is very large — there is a great deal of membrane for a very small amount of cytoplasm to supply. Oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide out quickly enough to keep every part of the organism supplied.

That stops working as an organism gets bigger, for a reason that is geometric rather than biological. **Surface area grows as a square** of the length, while **volume grows as a cube**. Volume therefore grows **faster**, and the ratio between them **falls**. Doubling the length of a cube multiplies its surface area by **4** but its volume by **8**, so the surface area to volume ratio **halves**.

The numbers show it plainly. A cube of side 1 cm has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, a ratio of **6 : 1**. A cube of side 4 cm has a surface area of 96 cm² and a volume of 64 cm³ — a ratio of only **1.5 : 1**. The larger cube has **four times less** surface for each unit of volume it must supply.

A large animal therefore faces two problems at once. It has proportionally **less surface** through which substances can enter and leave, and the **distance** from that surface to the cells in the middle is now far too great for diffusion, which is very slow over long distances.

The solution is two structures rather than one. **Exchange surfaces** such as the alveoli restore the surface area, being folded into millions of tiny sacs with walls one cell thick. A **transport system** — the circulatory system — then carries the substances the rest of the way, so that no cell has to rely on diffusion over more than a very short distance from the nearest capillary. Neither would be enough on its own.

A cube of side 4 cm has a surface area of 96 cm² and a volume of 64 cm³ — a ratio of only **1.5 : 1**. The larger cube has **four times less** surface for each unit of volume it must supply.

A large animal therefore faces two problems at once. It has proportionally **less surface** through which substances can enter and leave, and the **distance** from that surface to the cells in the middle is now far too great for diffusion, which is very slow over long distances.

The solution is two structures rather than one. **Exchange surfaces** such as the alveoli restore the surface area, being folded into millions of tiny sacs with walls one cell thick. A **transport system** — the circulatory system — then carries the substances the rest of the way, so that no cell has to rely on diffusion over more than a very short distance from the nearest capillary. Neither would be enough on its own.

questions.prompt: Describe how the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange, and explain each adaptation in terms of the factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
questions.solution:
The alveoli are adapted in four ways, and each one addresses a factor that affects the **rate of diffusion**.

First, there are **millions of alveoli**, which together give an enormous **surface area**. Surface area is on the **top** of Fick's law, so more of it means a **faster** rate: far more diffusion can happen at once than a single large sac of the same volume would allow.

Second, the **walls of the alveolus are one cell thick**, and the **capillary walls** beside them are also one cell thick. The gases therefore cross only two cells in total, giving a very **short diffusion distance**. Distance is on the **bottom** of Fick's law, so keeping it small keeps the rate **high**.

Third, the alveoli have a **rich blood supply**, a dense network of capillaries. This matters for a reason that is easy to state the wrong way round: the blood does not bring oxygen to the lungs, it **carries oxygen away**. By removing oxygen as fast as it arrives, the blood flow stops it building up and so **maintains a steep concentration gradient**.

Fourth, **ventilation** — breathing — continually **renews the air** in the alveoli, bringing in fresh oxygen and carrying away carbon dioxide. This does exactly the same job as the blood supply, but from the **air side** rather than the blood side. Both keep the **concentration difference** large, and concentration difference is also on the **top** of Fick's law.

The alveolar lining is also kept **moist**, because gases must **dissolve** before they can diffuse across a membrane.

Putting these together, the three factors — **surface area**, **diffusion distance** and **concentration gradient** — are each addressed in the most effective way the body can manage, which is why the adaptations are better understood as three ideas than as a list of five facts. It also explains disease: emphysema destroys alveolar walls and so reduces **surface area**, while pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid and so increases the **diffusion distance**. In both cases naming the factor that changed explains the symptom.

thin walls on both sides, giving a short diffusion distance
blood supply maintains the gradient
ventilation maintains the gradient
maps the adaptations onto the factors affecting diffusion

criteria.text: Large surface area from millions of alveoli, allowing more diffusion at once.

Ventilation, which renews the air and so also maintains the concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: A plant must take in water and mineral ions from the soil. Which cells are adapted to take them in?
questions.skill: exchange in a range of organisms
questions.solution: **Root hair cells on the surface of the root** take in water and mineral ions. Their long, thin extensions give a large surface area, which is the same answer to the surface area problem that the alveoli give in a lung.

questions.prompt: An exchange surface has a surface area of 70, a concentration difference of 3 and a membrane thickness of 0.5, all in arbitrary units. Use Fick's law to calculate the rate of diffusion in arbitrary units.
questions.skill: calculating a rate with Fick's law
questions.solution: Rate $\propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness}} = \dfrac{70 \times 3}{0.5} = \dfrac{210}{0.5} = 420$ arbitrary units. Dividing by 0.5 **doubles** the value, so a thin membrane gives a high rate. The answer has no real unit such as m/s, because Fick's law is a proportionality.

markScheme.description: substitutes 70 × 3 ÷ 0.5

questions.prompt: Oxygen moves into an animal's cells. Which of these substances moves out of the cells as a waste product of respiration?
questions.solution: **Carbon dioxide.** It is made by respiration in every cell and must be carried away and removed — in a mammal, by the blood to the lungs. Mineral ions and dissolved food molecules are taken **in**, and oxygen is taken in for respiration. The sixth substance on the specification's list, **urea**, is also a waste, from the breakdown of excess amino acids.

questions.prompt: One cube has sides of 1 cm and another has sides of 2 cm. How do their surface area to volume ratios compare?
questions.solution: Side 1 cm: surface area $6 \times 1 = 6$ cm², volume $1$ cm³, ratio **6 : 1**. Side 2 cm: surface area $6 \times 4 = 24$ cm², volume $8$ cm³, ratio **3 : 1**. Doubling the side multiplies the area by **4** but the volume by **8**, so the ratio **halves**: the small cube has twice the ratio of the large one. That is why the larger an organism is, the less surface it has for each unit of body to supply.

markScheme.description: the 1 cm cube has twice the ratio (6 : 1 against 3 : 1)

options: The 2 cm cube's ratio is twice that of the 1 cm cube
The 1 cm cube's ratio is four times that of the 2 cm cube
The 1 cm cube's ratio is twice that of the 2 cm cube
The two cubes have the same ratio, because both are cubes

questions.prompt: A fish keeps a continuous flow of water passing over its gills, which are its exchange surface. Which factor affecting the rate of diffusion does this maintain, and how?
questions.skill: applying the factors to an unfamiliar exchange surface
questions.solution: **The concentration gradient.** As oxygen diffuses from the water into the blood, the water next to the gill loses oxygen and the difference shrinks. Replacing it with fresh water keeps the difference **large**, so diffusion stays fast. It is the same job that **ventilation** does for the alveoli: renew the supply on one side while the **blood flow** carries oxygen away on the other. Moving water does not change the surface area or the thickness of the gill, and temperature is not one of the three factors.

markScheme.description: the concentration gradient, by replacing water that has lost its oxygen

options: The surface area: moving water makes the gill filaments grow longer
The diffusion distance: moving water presses the gill membrane thinner
The temperature: moving water keeps the gills cooler than the blood
The concentration gradient: water that has lost its oxygen is replaced

questions.prompt: A student says that halving the thickness of an exchange surface would have the same effect on the rate of diffusion as doubling its surface area. Is the student right?
questions.solution: **Yes.** In Fick's law, rate $\propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness}}$. Doubling the surface area doubles the top, so the rate doubles. Halving the thickness halves the bottom, and dividing by half as much **also doubles** the rate. The two changes have the same effect because the law is a proportionality: it multiplies and divides, it does not add, and nothing in it is squared.

markScheme.description: yes: halving the thickness doubles the rate, as doubling the area does

options: No: thickness is on the bottom of Fick's law, so it has a much smaller effect
Yes: halving the thickness doubles the rate, just as doubling the area does
No: surface area is squared in Fick's law, so it has the bigger effect
Yes: both changes add the same fixed amount to the rate of diffusion

questions.prompt: Name the system that transports substances around a mammal's body once they have crossed an exchange surface.
questions.solution: **The circulatory system** — the heart, the blood vessels and the blood. An exchange surface such as the lungs gets substances across a membrane, but in a large organism diffusion would be far too slow to carry them to every cell, so a transport system does the rest of the journey.

markScheme.description: the circulatory (blood) system

questions.prompt: A block of agar jelly measures 2 cm by 2 cm by 4 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio. Give the ratio in the form n : 1 and enter n.
questions.skill: surface area to volume of a block
questions.solution: The block has two faces of $2 \times 2 = 4$ cm² and four faces of $2 \times 4 = 8$ cm², so the surface area is $(2 \times 4) + (4 \times 8) = 8 + 32 = 40$ cm². The volume is $2 \times 2 \times 4 = 16$ cm³. The ratio is $\dfrac{40}{16} = 2.5$, written **2.5 : 1**.

markScheme.description: surface area 40 cm² and volume 16 cm³

questions.prompt: A healthy exchange surface has a surface area of 60, a concentration difference of 5 and a membrane thickness of 2, all in arbitrary units. A disease reduces the surface area to 45 and makes the membrane 3 units thick, while the concentration difference stays at 5. Use Fick's law, rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of membrane, to calculate the percentage decrease in the rate of diffusion.
questions.solution: Healthy: rate $\propto \dfrac{60 \times 5}{2} = \dfrac{300}{2} = 150$ arbitrary units. Diseased: $\dfrac{45 \times 5}{3} = \dfrac{225}{3} = 75$ arbitrary units. The decrease is $150 - 75 = 75$, and $\dfrac{75}{150} \times 100 = 50$ %. Both changes work the same way: less area on the top and more thickness on the bottom each slow diffusion, and together they halve the rate.

markScheme.description: rates of 150 and 75 arbitrary units
decrease divided by the original rate, × 100

questions.prompt: Explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse across the wall of an alveolus in opposite directions at the same time.
questions.solution: Each gas diffuses **down its own concentration gradient**, independently of the other. Oxygen is **higher** in the air in the alveolus than in the blood, so it moves **into** the blood; carbon dioxide is **higher** in the blood than in the air, so it moves **out**. The two gradients run in opposite directions, so the two gases do too.

markScheme.description: each gas diffuses down its own concentration gradient
oxygen is higher in the air than the blood, carbon dioxide higher in the blood than the air

criteria.text: Each gas diffuses down its own concentration gradient, independently of the other
Oxygen is more concentrated in the air in the alveolus than in the blood, so it moves into the blood; carbon dioxide is more concentrated in the blood than in the air, so it moves out

questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion is the net movement of a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated, and each substance moves down its own gradient without being affected by any other. Blood arriving at the alveolus has come from the tissues, so it is low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide. The air in the alveolus, freshly breathed in, is high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide. So oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air, both at the same time and across the same thin wall, simply because the two gradients run in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: A baby born several weeks early has lungs that are not fully developed: it has fewer alveoli than a full-term baby, and the walls of its alveoli are thicker. Explain, using the factors that affect the rate of diffusion, why such a baby may be given air containing extra oxygen.
questions.skill: applying the factors to an unfamiliar case
questions.solution: Fewer alveoli mean a **smaller surface area**, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood at once. Thicker walls mean a **longer diffusion distance**, so oxygen crosses more slowly. Both are on the wrong side of Fick's law for the baby. Air with extra oxygen raises the **concentration difference** between the air and the blood — the one factor that can be changed from outside — which speeds diffusion up and makes up for the other two.

thicker walls: longer diffusion distance, so slower diffusion
extra oxygen increases the concentration difference, which raises the rate

questions.modelAnswer: The rate of diffusion depends on three factors: surface area, concentration gradient and diffusion distance. In Fick's law, surface area and concentration difference are on the top and thickness is on the bottom. The baby's lungs are worse off on two of the three. Fewer alveoli give a smaller surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse across into the blood at any moment. Thicker alveolar walls give a longer diffusion distance, so each oxygen molecule takes longer to cross. Together these make the rate of gas exchange too low to supply the baby's cells from ordinary air. The one factor that can be changed from outside is the concentration difference. Air containing extra oxygen has a much higher oxygen concentration than the blood arriving at the alveoli, so the difference between the two sides is larger and oxygen diffuses faster, which makes up for the smaller area and longer distance until the lungs have developed.

questions.prompt: A student cuts cubes of agar jelly containing an indicator, with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm, drops them into dilute acid and times how long the acid takes to change the colour of the whole cube. Describe how the student should carry out this investigation so that it is a fair test, predict the results using surface area to volume ratios, and explain what the results show about why large organisms need exchange surfaces.
questions.skill: surface area to volume in a model investigation
questions.solution: The ratios are 6 : 1 for the 1 cm cube, 3 : 1 for the 2 cm cube and 2 : 1 for the 3 cm cube, so the ratio falls as the cube grows. For a fair test, keep the acid concentration, its volume, the temperature and the type of agar the same, judge the end point the same way for every cube (no colour left at the centre), and repeat each size for a mean. Prediction: the 3 cm cube takes longest, because the acid has furthest to travel to its centre and there is least surface for each unit of volume. The cubes model organisms: as an organism gets bigger its surface area to volume ratio falls and the distance to its middle grows, so diffusion alone cannot supply its cells. A large organism therefore needs exchange surfaces with a large area and thin walls, such as alveoli, and a transport system to carry substances the rest of the way.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some steps of the method or a ratio calculated, with little explanation
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a fair-test method with the ratios compared and a mostly correct prediction, with some links to organisms
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent account linking the controlled method, the ratios, the prediction and the need for exchange surfaces and a transport system

questions.modelAnswer:
The cubes have very different surface area to volume ratios. The 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, a ratio of 6 : 1. The 2 cm cube has 24 cm² and 8 cm³, a ratio of 3 : 1. The 3 cm cube has 54 cm² and 27 cm³, a ratio of 2 : 1. Surface area grows as a square and volume as a cube, so the bigger the cube, the less surface it has for each cubic centimetre inside it.

To make the test fair, the independent variable is the size of the cube and the dependent variable is the time for the acid to reach the centre. I would use the same concentration and the same volume of acid for each cube, at the same temperature, cut from the same block of agar, and start the stopwatch as each cube went in. The hardest part is deciding when the colour has gone from the whole cube, so I would use the same rule every time, for example the moment no colour is left at the very centre, and have the same person judge it. I would repeat each size three times and use the mean, discarding any anomalous time.

I would predict that the 1 cm cube changes colour fastest and the 3 cm cube slowest. The acid has to diffuse 0.5 cm to reach the centre of the small cube but 1.5 cm to reach the centre of the large one, and the large cube also has the least surface through which acid can enter for each unit of volume that must be reached.

The cubes are a model of organisms. A single-celled organism is like the small cube: everything is close to the surface and its ratio is large, so diffusion alone supplies it. A large animal is like the big cube, only far more so: its surface area to volume ratio is tiny and its cells are a long way from the outside, so oxygen could never diffuse in fast enough. That is why it needs specialised exchange surfaces with a very large area and thin walls, such as the alveoli, together with a transport system, the blood, to carry substances the rest of the way to every cell.

examTechnique.body:
Two skills are examined here and they support each other. The **calculation** — surface area to volume — is the argument for why exchange surfaces exist at all, so it is worth being able to produce the numbers rather than only quoting the conclusion.

The **explanation** half is always adaptation plus reason. Every alveolus adaptation maps onto one of three factors: **surface area**, **diffusion distance**, or **concentration gradient**. Answer by naming the factor, and unfamiliar cases — a disease, a fish gill, an insect — become questions you have already practised.
examinerErrors: Explaining why large organisms need lungs by saying they *need more oxygen*, rather than by the **surface area to volume ratio**.
Calculating the surface area of a cube with **four** faces instead of **six**.
Giving an adaptation without its **reason**, when the question asks for an explanation.
Saying the blood supply **brings oxygen to** the lungs rather than **carrying it away** to maintain the gradient.
Treating **thickness** in Fick's law as though it were on the **top**, which reverses the answer.
Attaching a real unit such as **m/s** to a rate worked out from Fick's law, when the relationship is only a **proportionality** and the rate is in **arbitrary units**.
Writing the ratio as volume to surface area, so it rises rather than falls with size.
Answering a disease question without naming **which** factor has changed.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer proves the ratio claim rather than asserting it: **area grows as a square, volume as a cube**, so doubling the side gives **×4** and **×8** and the ratio **halves** — with numbers to show it. It gives the reason with every adaptation, and recognises that **blood supply and ventilation are one idea**, maintaining the gradient from opposite sides. In Fick's law it reads position as direction, checks itself with the case where doubling area and thickness **cancels**, and answers in **factors**, or in **arbitrary units** when values are substituted, never in a real unit. Faced with emphysema, pneumonia or an unfamiliar organism, it names **which of the three factors** has changed and reasons from there.
